## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kāmavilāpajātaka* (Ja 297) is a birth-tale belonging to the Jātaka collection of the Pali Canon [Catalog]. According to the traditional framework, the Buddha recounted this story while residing at Jetavana with reference to a monk pining for his former wife; the commentary cross-references the background context of the present to the *Puppharattajātaka* and the tale of the past to the *Indriyajātaka* [Fausböll 1879]. In the story, a man impaled on a stake (*jīvasūla*) in mortal danger laments and dispatches a crow as an envoy carrying a message to his wife before dying and being reborn in hell [Fausböll 1879; Louis de la Vallée Poussin memorial volume]. Upon hearing the teaching and the exposition of the Four Noble Truths, the longing monk attains the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*), and the Buddha identifies himself as the deity who witnessed the event [Fausböll 1879].

In comparative literary analysis, the narrative device in the *Kāmavilāpajātaka*—in which an imperiled husband sends a bird messenger to his wife—has been discussed alongside classical Indian messenger poetry such as Kālidāsa's *Meghadūta* [Louis de la Vallée Poussin memorial volume].

 DharmaNexus identifies text reuse entirely within Pali literature, sharing segments (§1.1–3.4) with the second volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].
